theme: In you, O LORD, do I take refuge, the prayer of the aging saint
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 71. This is the prayer of an old believer, looking back on a lifetime of God’s faithfulness and forward to the end. Read it slowly, as if praying it for a grandparent, or for yourself in forty years.
settingTheScene: Psalm 71 has no title, but it follows Psalm 70 and reads like a continuation. The writer has trusted God from youth and now faces old age and enemies. Many in the second temple community, old men who had seen the first temple, would have prayed it. It is the great psalm of lifelong faith.
observation: “In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame!” (v. 1).
“Be to me a rock of refuge, to which I may continually come” (v. 3).
“For you, O Lord, are my hope, my trust, O LORD, from my youth” (v. 5).
“Do not cast me off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength is spent” (v. 9).
“But I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more” (v. 14).
“O God, from my youth you have taught me, and I still proclaim your wondrous deeds” (v. 17).
“So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation” (v. 18).
“You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again” (v. 20).
interpretation:
This is an elder’s prayer. The speaker has relied on God since birth: “Upon you I have leaned from before my birth; you are he who took me from my mother’s womb.” God has been faithful through every season. Yet old age brings new fears: “Do not cast me off in the time of old age.” Strength is ebbing, and enemies see weakness as an opportunity: “God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him.”

The psalmist’s answer is not despair but renewed praise. “I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more.” Hope grows rather than fades. His mouth will tell of God’s righteous acts all day long, “for their number is past my knowledge.” He cannot count them all.

The center of the psalm is verse 18. The old man asks for continued life with a purpose: “until I proclaim your might to another generation, your power to all those to come.” This is what old age is for. The aim of long life is not comfort but testimony. Those who have walked with God for decades are a treasure to the church. They have seen troubles and calamities, and they can say, “God brought me through.”

The psalm ends with confidence: “You will revive me again.” The one who made him see many troubles will bring him up from the depths. There is a note here that reaches beyond this life, toward resurrection. And the final word is praise, with harp, lyre, and lips that shout for joy.

For the young, the psalm is a challenge: build a life of trust now, so that you can pray this in old age. For the old, it is a comfort.
connection: Isaiah 46:4: “Even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you.” Titus 2:2-5 charges older believers to teach the younger. 2 Corinthians 4:16: “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.” Psalm 92:14: the righteous “still bear fruit in old age.” 2 Timothy 4:7-8: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race.” Deuteronomy 6:7: teach your children.
application:
Call or visit an older believer and ask them to tell you how God has been faithful to them.

If you are older, write down three stories of God’s faithfulness to pass on.

Pray verse 18 for yourself: “Let me proclaim your might to another generation.”
prayerPrompts: Thank God for being your hope from youth.
Ask him not to cast you away when you are old or weak.
Pray for the generation that comes after you.
